name: Carotid arteries
func: The main arteries running up each side of the neck. They deliver most of the blood to the brain, eyes, face and scalp, and sensors in their walls help control blood pressure and breathing.

levels.kid:
Put two fingers gently on the side of your neck, just beside your windpipe. Feel that thump-thump? That's your **carotid artery**!

You have two, one on each side of your neck. They're big blood tubes carrying fresh, oxygen-filled blood up from your heart to your head.

Near the top of your neck, each one splits in two, like a road fork. One branch goes inside your skull to feed your brain, which needs tons of blood to think. The other branch feeds your face, your tongue and your scalp.

The carotids are super important, because your brain gets most of its blood from them.
levels.hs:
Each **common carotid artery** runs up the neck inside a protective tube of tissue called the **carotid sheath**, together with the **internal jugular vein** (on its outer side) and the **vagus nerve** (behind, between the two). The right one starts from the **brachiocephalic trunk**; the left comes straight off the **aortic arch**.

At about the level of the upper border of the **thyroid cartilage** (Adam's apple), around **C3–C4**, it divides into:

The **external carotid artery (ECA)**, which supplies the face, scalp, tongue, throat and the coverings of the brain through branches such as the **facial**, **lingual**, **superficial temporal** and **maxillary** arteries. (The maxillary gives the **middle meningeal artery**.)

The **internal carotid artery (ICA)**, which has **no branches in the neck**. It enters the skull through the **carotid canal** in the temporal bone and supplies most of the front and middle of the brain, plus the eye via the **ophthalmic artery**.

At the split, the ICA has a swelling called the **carotid sinus**, which senses blood pressure, and a tiny organ called the **carotid body**, which senses oxygen levels in the blood.
levels.college:
The ICA is described in segments (Bouthillier classification, C1–C7): **cervical**, **petrous** (in the carotid canal), **lacerum**, **cavernous** (inside the cavernous sinus, alongside cranial nerve VI and with III, IV, V1 and V2 in the lateral wall), **clinoid**, **ophthalmic** and **communicating**. The S-shaped bends of its cavernous and supraclinoid parts form the **carotid siphon**, visible on angiograms.

Intracranial branches include the **ophthalmic artery**, the **posterior communicating artery (PComm)**, the **anterior choroidal artery** and finally the terminal split into the **anterior** and **middle cerebral arteries**. Through the PComm and the anterior communicating artery, the carotids join the vertebrobasilar system in the **circle of Willis**.

**Baroreceptor** reflex: stretch of the carotid sinus wall sends signals along the **glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)** (via the carotid sinus nerve of Hering) to the **nucleus tractus solitarius** in the medulla, which slows the heart and dilates vessels. The aortic arch baroreceptors use the vagus. The **carotid body** (glomus cells) responds mainly to low arterial oxygen, increasing breathing.

The ECA and ICA have important **anastomoses**, for example via the ophthalmic artery around the orbit; in chronic ICA blockage these can reverse and supply the brain.
levels.phd:
Carotid atherosclerosis concentrates at the **bifurcation**, especially the outer wall of the carotid bulb, where flow separates and creates **low, oscillatory wall shear stress**. Endothelial cells sense shear through mechanosensors (**PECAM-1/VE-cadherin/VEGFR2** complexes, **Piezo1**, primary cilia) and, under disturbed flow, activate **NF-κB** and suppress protective **KLF2/KLF4** programs. That's why plaques form on the outside of the bend rather than the flow-divider.

Stroke risk is about plaque **composition**, not only narrowing: **intraplaque hemorrhage**, a **lipid-rich necrotic core** and a **thin or ruptured fibrous cap** predict events and can be imaged with high-resolution vessel-wall MRI. Emboli of platelet aggregates or cholesterol travel into the ICA territory; small cholesterol crystals lodged at retinal artery branch points are visible as **Hollenhorst plaques**.

The **carotid body** is the body's main peripheral oxygen sensor. Its **type I (glomus) cells** depolarize in hypoxia: mitochondrial complex I signaling and inhibition of oxygen-sensitive potassium channels lead to calcium entry and release of transmitters (notably ATP, acting on P2X receptors on afferent fibers). Slower, gene-level oxygen sensing in all cells (the **HIF** pathway) won the 2019 Nobel Prize; the carotid body's second-by-second response is a separate, faster mechanism.

Embryologically, the common carotid and proximal ICA come from the **third pharyngeal arch arteries**, the distal ICA from the paired **dorsal aortae**. Persistent embryonic carotid–basilar connections, such as a **persistent trigeminal artery**, are occasional angiographic findings.
levels.expert:
A **carotid bruit** (whooshing sound over the neck) may signal stenosis but is an unreliable guide to severity. Symptoms of ICA territory ischemia: contralateral weakness or numbness, **aphasia** (dominant hemisphere), neglect (non-dominant), and **amaurosis fugax**, a transient "curtain" over vision in the **same-side eye** from emboli to the ophthalmic artery.

Imaging: **duplex ultrasound** first, then **CT or MR angiography**; digital subtraction angiography is the gold standard. Symptomatic stenosis of about 70–99% clearly benefits from **carotid endarterectomy** (NASCET), ideally within two weeks of symptoms; 50–69% has a smaller benefit. **Carotid artery stenting** is an alternative in selected patients.

During endarterectomy, surgeons protect the **hypoglossal nerve (XII)** (tongue deviation if injured), the **vagus** and its recurrent laryngeal branch (hoarseness), and the **marginal mandibular** branch of the facial nerve. Post-operative **hyperperfusion syndrome** can cause headache, seizures and intracerebral hemorrhage.

**Carotid dissection** after neck trauma or even minor twisting causes neck pain, an ipsilateral **Horner syndrome** (sympathetic fibers run on the ICA) and stroke. A **carotid–cavernous fistula** causes a pulsating bulging eye, a red eye and a bruit over the orbit; it's treated endovascularly. **Cavernous carotid aneurysms** can compress cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI.

**Carotid sinus massage** can slow the heart and is used to treat some fast heart rhythms, but is avoided in people with a carotid bruit because it can dislodge plaque. Treatment in general terms: antiplatelets, statins, blood pressure control, and revascularization when indicated.

keyPoints: Common carotid splits into internal and external at about C3–C4
Internal carotid has no neck branches; feeds most of the brain and the eye
Carotid sheath: carotid artery, internal jugular vein, vagus nerve
Carotid sinus = pressure sensor (CN IX); carotid body = oxygen sensor
Amaurosis fugax: transient same-side vision loss from carotid emboli

test.q: Which branch of the common carotid has NO branches in the neck?
test.explain: The ICA runs up to the skull base without branching; the ECA branches freely in the neck and face.

test.q: Which cranial nerve carries signals from the carotid sinus baroreceptors?
test.explain: The carotid sinus nerve (of Hering) is a branch of CN IX to the medulla.

test.q: Transient monocular vision loss from carotid emboli is called:
test.explain: Emboli travel to the ophthalmic artery (first branch of the ICA) and briefly blind the same-side eye.

test.q: Which structure is NOT in the carotid sheath?
test.explain: The phrenic nerve lies on scalenus anterior, outside the sheath.

test.q: Carotid dissection can damage sympathetic fibers on the ICA, causing ______ syndrome.
test.explain: Ptosis, a small pupil and sometimes reduced sweating on the same side.

test.q: A surgeon doing carotid endarterectomy who injures the hypoglossal nerve will see:
choices: Tongue deviation toward the injured side
test.explain: Weak genioglossus on one side lets the tongue deviate toward the lesion when protruded.
